questions.q: Why do triple-barrier (or other forward-looking) labels tend to overlap in time?
options: Because the labels are randomly shuffled before training
Because each label's outcome depends on a window of several future bars, so consecutive labels' windows can cover the same bars
Because the data was collected twice
Because of floating-point rounding errors
questions.explain: Each label looks forward across a window of bars to determine its outcome; consecutive labels' windows frequently cover the same stretch of time, creating overlap.

questions.q: What standard machine learning assumption does overlapping label windows violate?
options: That features must be normalized
That training examples are independent and identically distributed (IID)
That the target variable must be continuous
That the model must be linear
questions.explain: Overlapping windows mean nearby labels are correlated with each other rather than independent draws, violating the IID assumption most ML algorithms rely on.

questions.q: What does 'concurrency' measure in this context?
options: The number of CPU threads used during training
How many labels' outcome windows cover a given point in time
The correlation between two different assets
The number of features in the dataset
questions.explain: Concurrency at a given bar counts how many labels' windows span that bar -- a key input to computing average uniqueness.

questions.q: How does average-uniqueness weighting address the overlap problem?
options: It deletes all overlapping labels from the dataset
It weights each label roughly inversely to how much its window overlaps with others, so heavily overlapping labels don't dominate training
It converts the problem into an unsupervised learning task
It increases the learning rate for overlapping labels
questions.explain: A label with high overlap gets a smaller weight (closer to 0), while a largely unique label gets a weight near 1, preventing overlapping observations from being over-counted.

questions.q: Where do average-uniqueness weights get applied when training a scikit-learn or XGBoost model?
options: In the `random_state` parameter
In the `sample_weight` argument of the model's `.fit()` method
They cannot be used with tree-based models
In the `test_size` parameter of train_test_split
questions.explain: Both scikit-learn and XGBoost (and LightGBM) accept a `sample_weight` argument in `.fit()`, which is where average-uniqueness weights are passed in.
